slides.title: clim°: storm insurance for Uniswap v4 LPs
slides.text: clim°. Storm insurance for Uniswap v4 LPs. clim-zeta.vercel.app. DeVinci Blockchain × TOKEN2049 Origins Hackathon, 6 to 8 October 2026. Built on Chainlink and Uniswap.
slides.notes:
Hi, I am Sofiane, from DeVinci Blockchain. This is clim°: storm insurance for the people who provide liquidity on Uniswap v4, the liquidity providers, or LPs. I built it on Chainlink CRE and Uniswap v4 for TOKEN2049 Origins, and it is live on the Sepolia testnet at clim-zeta.vercel.app. Keep the pink spiral in mind: it is the same storm that runs on the app's screen, because the whole idea is that the fee follows the weather.

Sources (not read aloud): live app https://clim-zeta.vercel.app (liveUrl in docs/submission/links.json); code https://github.com/DVB-ANS/clim. The deck has 10 slides and no appendix; the details are in these notes: the fee rule (slide 05), the limits of the backtest, the 7 October live storm and the 4 February 2026 lab replay as backup (05), safety, the CRE evidence and the limits of the live build (07), why Chainlink CRE, the trust condition on a DON and our feedback to Chainlink (09), whether a pool that is already live can switch, the roadmap and the team (10). Slide 08 embeds the 30-second stage cut of the demo video; the full demo video is the submission's Project link.

slides.title: Where the idea comes from
slides.text: Fables on Robinhood Chain. Liquidity providers earned fees. Arbitrage took back 75 to 105 %. Bar chart: fees earned; lost to arbitrage, 75 to 105 % of them. ETH/USDG, 14 days. Pre-hackathon research, 30 Sept 2026.
slides.notes:
This idea did not start on a whiteboard. Before the hackathon, I measured 14 days of Fables' ETH/USDG pool on Robinhood Chain, in September, against three external prices that agreed. Depending on the method, arbitrage took back 75 to 105 % of the fees the liquidity providers earned. Researchers call that loss loss-versus-rebalancing, or LVR. When ETH jumps on Binance, arbitrage bots buy from the pool at the old price, and the LP pays the gap. That loss grows with the square of volatility: at the same trading volume, double the volatility means about four times the loss. Fables' keeper does raise the pool's fee when the market moves, and over those 14 days the LPs still gave most or all of their fees back. This is pre-hackathon research, not a result of the hack. It is why clim exists: the fee did not keep up with the weather. Every AMM has this problem; Fables' pool is simply where I measured it.

Sources (not read aloud): research note dated 2026-09-30, summarized in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-06-clim-design.md section 1.3 (external mids from Coinbase, Lighter and Hyperliquid); Milionis, Moallemi, Roughgarden and Zhang (2022), Automated Market Making and Loss-Versus-Rebalancing, arXiv:2208.06046 (LVR grows with the square of volatility); "about four times the loss" is an illustration at equal volume, not a measurement. Fables' fee is not flat: a keeper pokes it between a floor and a cap, and it follows volatility (lab/README.md, "clim vs Fables' keeper": correlation 0.83 with Binance RV15 over 31 days under its current config, from 2026-09-06; first poke 2026-08-23, so the keeper was live during the 14 days measured).

slides.title: Why LPs lose: when ETH jumps, the fastest bots win
slides.text: When ETH jumps, the fastest bots win. A pool only changes its price when someone trades with it. ETH jumps on Binance: the real price moves first. Bots buy at the old price: the fastest trade takes the difference. The LP pays the gap: small when calm, huge in a storm. Researchers call this loss LVR, loss-versus-rebalancing. The fee is the only thing a pool charges for it.
slides.notes:
Here is what I saw in that data. A pool only changes its price when someone trades with it. When ETH jumps on Binance, the pool still shows the old price for a moment, and the fastest bots buy there and sell on Binance. The liquidity providers pay that difference. Researchers call it loss-versus-rebalancing, or LVR. It is small when the market is calm and huge in a storm, and the fee is the only thing the pool charges for it.

Sources (not read aloud): LVR as defined by Milionis, Moallemi, Roughgarden and Zhang (2022), cited in the README and spec section 2; the 75 to 105 % on slide 02 is the pre-hackathon research of 30 September 2026 (Fables ETH/USDG on Robinhood Chain, 14 days, against three external prices); the per-block arbitrage model is Milionis, Moallemi and Roughgarden (2023) and Nezlobin and Tassy (2025) (spec section 2.3).

slides.title: Backed by TradFi practice
slides.text: Backed by TradFi practice. A trading desk prices risk from volatility and volume, and quotes wider in a storm. TradFi, a trading desk: a risk desk reads volatility and volume; traders quote wider in a storm; calm days stay cheap. clim° on a DEX: Chainlink CRE reads the weather; the pool's fee rises in a storm; calm days stay at 5 bp. 6 October, day 1 of the hackathon: on a DEX, the price of liquidity is the fee.
slides.notes:
So I looked at how TradFi prices this risk. A trading desk does not quote the same price in every weather: its risk desk reads volatility and volume, and its traders quote wider in a storm, with methods that market makers have used for decades. On a DEX, the price of liquidity is the fee. That became the idea on the first day of the hackathon, 6 October, and its name: clim, the market's weather. Chainlink CRE reads the weather, the pool's fee rises in a storm, and it stays at 5 basis points when the market is calm.

Sources (not read aloud): market-making references: Glosten and Milgrom (1985), the spread pays for adverse selection by informed traders; Avellaneda and Stoikov (2008), quotes from volatility, inventory and order flow; the slow risk desk and fast quoting engine split is the design's TradFi idea (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-06-clim-design.md, section 1); the name and the product were decided on 6 October (docs/sessions/2026-10-06.md, Decisions); the 5 bp calm fee is feeMinPips 500 in shared/params.json, the pair's usual fee tier; volume next to volatility: README Roadmap item 4 and docs/faq.md, "Why not set the fee from volume too?".

slides.title: The idea: the fee follows the weather
slides.text: The fee follows the weather. When prices move, speed costs more. The premium goes to LPs. Chart: fee per swap against ETH volatility per year: calm, 5 bp; 100 %, 10.95 bp; storm, 225 %, 24.63 bp. 1 bp = 0.01 % of each trade.
slides.notes:
An LP is an insurer: it sells protection to traders, and the fee is its premium. That is the storm insurance on the cover: with clim, the premium finally covers the storm. When prices move, the fastest traders, arbitrage bots racing to the pool's stale price, are the ones who profit at the LP's expense: clim makes that speed cost more in a storm, and the extra fee goes to the LPs. When the market is calm, the fee is the pair's usual tier, 5 basis points, that is 0.05 % of each trade, so traders pay what the pool next door charges. Above about 46 % annualized volatility, the fee rises in proportion: 10.95 basis points at 100 %, 24.63 at 225 %. This is the exact schedule of the hook deployed on Sepolia. The rule fits on one line: eta times sigma times the square root of half a block, between a floor of 5 and a cap of 150 basis points. Sigma times the square root of half a block is the typical price move while an arbitrageur waits. Eta says how many of those moves the fee covers: with eta equal to one over P-star minus 0.824, a block gets arbitraged with probability P-star once the fee is above the floor. The lab chose P-star of 30 %, so eta is 2.51, against a competing 5 basis point pool, before deployment, because the hook's parameters are immutable.

Sources (not read aloud): README section "Fee schedule", computed from shared/params.json (P* = 30 %, etaE4 25093, floor 500 pips, cap 15000 pips, k = 1). The rule: fee = clamp(η · k · σ · √(Δt/2), floor, cap), with σ the desk's 15-minute realized volatility, η = 1/P* − 0.824 = 2.51, Δt the 12 s Sepolia block, k a model-risk multiplier bounded to [1, 2] (k = 1 in this build), floor 5 bp (the pair's usual tier) and cap 150 bp; on-chain integer arithmetic: fee_pips = clamp(ceil(sigmaE9 × etaE4 × sqrtHalfDtE6 × kE4 / 1e17), 500, 15000) in contracts/src/libraries/ClimFeeMath.sol; P* decided by lab/scripts/decide_pstar.py (decidedBy in shared/params.json); Milionis, Moallemi and Roughgarden (2023), arXiv:2305.14604; Nezlobin and Tassy (2025), arXiv:2505.05113.

slides.title: How it works: nobody changes the fee by hand
slides.text: Nobody changes the fee by hand. Each pool is created with its keeper; Chainlink CRE feeds it every 30 s. 4 exchanges, then Chainlink CRE (CRE workflow: every 30 s, the median of the four), then the risk desk (one number, on-chain), then the Uniswap v4 hook (the keeper: prices every swap). Sepolia testnet. CRE in simulation.
slides.notes:
Every 30 seconds, a Chainlink CRE workflow reads one-minute ETH prices from Coinbase, Kraken, Binance and Hyperliquid and takes their median, minute by minute. At least three of the four must have fresh prices, or there is no report. If one of them is more than 25 basis points away from the median, the report is flagged degraded and the hook charges at least its 30 basis point safe fee. From the median, the workflow computes one number: how stormy the market is right now, the 15-minute realized volatility. That number is written on-chain to my risk desk contract. Each pool is created with its keeper, here the Uniswap v4 hook, and Chainlink CRE feeds it. On every swap, Uniswap calls the hook, which reads the desk and returns the fee for that swap only: no admin call and no fee-update transaction. A DEX that already runs its own keeper, like Fables, can feed it from the same desk. On a Chainlink network of nodes (a DON), the nodes would agree on the median and sign one report; today one simulated node does it, on the Sepolia testnet.

Sources (not read aloud): workflow cre/risk-desk/workflow.ts and cre/risk-desk/estimator.ts (cron 30 s, HTTP, per-minute median of the fresh venues, quorum 3 of 4 or no report, ConsensusAggregationByFields median, EVMClient.writeReport); contracts/src/RiskDesk.sol (MIN_SOURCES = 3; flag DEGRADED when a venue is more than DISP_MAX_BP = 25 bp from the median) and contracts/src/ClimHook.sol (beforeSwap with OVERRIDE_FEE_FLAG; safe fee 3000 pips when degraded or blind); this slide answers the Chainlink mentor's first question on 6 October, how the fee is computed and who changes it (docs/faq.md, "How is the fee computed?" and "Who changes the fee, and how?"); DON deploy access requested on 2026-10-06 and not granted during the hackathon, so the DON deployment was cut.

slides.title: The fee: a keeper fed by CRE
slides.text: The fee: a keeper fed by CRE. Each pool is created with a keeper. Chainlink CRE is its only input. A new Uniswap v4 pool, created with clim°: Chainlink CRE (the workflow, every 30 s), then RiskDesk (σ written on-chain), then the keeper, the v4 hook (reads σ on every swap), then the fee (for this swap only). A DEX that already runs a keeper, like Fables: Chainlink CRE (the same workflow), then RiskDesk (the same desk), then their keeper (reads the desk, posts the fee), then the fee (until the next update). Nobody types a fee: it moves only when CRE's input moves. If CRE goes quiet for 180 s, the hook charges its 30 bp safe fee. Fables: our proposal, not an agreement.
slides.notes:
So how does the fee actually change? Each pool is created with a keeper, and the keeper has one input: Chainlink CRE's output. On a new Uniswap v4 pool, the keeper is the clim hook: every 30 seconds the CRE workflow writes the volatility to the risk desk, and on every swap the hook reads it and returns the fee for that swap only. Nobody types a fee, and no transaction changes it. A DEX that already runs a keeper, like Fables, plugs in the same way: its keeper reads the same desk and posts the fee, with its own floor and cap. And if CRE goes quiet for three minutes, the hook stops trusting old weather and charges its 30 basis point safe fee.

Sources (not read aloud): contracts/src/ClimHook.sol (beforeSwap returns the fee with OVERRIDE_FEE_FLAG; blind after tauKill 180 s, safe fee 3000 pips) and contracts/src/RiskDesk.sol (state()); cre/risk-desk/workflow.ts (30 s cron, writeReport to RiskDesk); docs/faq.md, "Who changes the fee, and how?" and "Can a pool that is already live switch to clim?" (a v4 pool's hook is fixed at creation, so clim means a new pool; a DEX whose keeper posts the fee can read the desk without migrating); README Roadmap item 1 and spec section 5.6 (Fables' keeper posts fee overrides between a floor and a cap; our proposal, not an agreement: nothing runs on Robinhood Chain yet).

slides.title: Two inputs: volatility and volume
slides.text: Two inputs: volatility and volume. Priced like a market maker: storms and one-way flow cost more. fee = clamp( η · σ · √(Δt/2) · k , 5 bp, 150 bp ). σ, volatility, live today: Chainlink CRE measures it every 30 s: the 15-minute realized volatility of the median ETH price on 4 exchanges. A storm raises the fee; a calm market pays the usual 5 bp. Loss-versus-rebalancing: Milionis, Moallemi and Roughgarden (2023). k, volume and flow, next: the same CRE workflow reads the pool's own swaps. Thin volume: a lower fee brings traders back. One-way, informed flow: a higher fee. Market making: Glosten and Milgrom (1985), Avellaneda and Stoikov (2008). Today k = 1, and RiskDesk clamps it to [1, 2], so volume can only raise the fee. Lowering it needs a new desk and hook, backtested first.
slides.notes:
The fee has two inputs, priced the way a market maker prices risk. The first is live today: volatility. Chainlink CRE measures the 15-minute realized volatility of ETH's median price on four exchanges, every 30 seconds; a storm raises the fee, and a calm market pays the usual 5 basis points. The formula comes from the research on loss-versus-rebalancing. The second input is volume. The same CRE workflow reads the pool's own swaps: when volume is thin, a lower fee brings traders back, and when one-way, informed flow dominates, the fee rises, as in the classic market-making models. It enters through k, the multiplier the desk already sends with every report, so the hook does not change. Today k is 1, and the desk clamps it between 1 and 2, so volume could only raise the fee; lowering it needs a new desk and hook, and I would backtest it against the same fixed-fee pool first.

Sources (not read aloud): the fee rule in contracts/src/libraries/ClimFeeMath.sol and shared/params.json (η = 1/P* − 0.824 = 2.509 at P* = 0.3, Δt = 12 s, floor 500 pips, cap 15,000 pips, k in RiskDesk's report, K_MIN_E4 and K_MAX_E4 clamp it to [1, 2]); Milionis, Moallemi and Roughgarden (2023) and Nezlobin and Tassy (2025) for the arbitrage model; the volume design: README Roadmap item 4, spec section 12 and docs/faq.md, "Why not set the fee from volume too?" (the workflow would read the pool's recent swaps with CRE's EVM client, separate arbitrage from uninformed flow and move k); Glosten and Milgrom (1985), Avellaneda and Stoikov (2008), Hasbrouck, Rivera and Saleh (2022).

slides.title: Does it work: LPs lose less, and the prediction can be checked
slides.text: LPs lose less to arbitrage. One-year lab backtest against a fixed-fee pool, on 1-minute ETH prices bridged to 12 s blocks. −27 % at the same average fee. −13 % at the same cost to traders. And it predicts how often it gets arbitraged. Share of blocks arbitraged, predicted and observed: Feb 2026 storm, 29.9 % and 27.9 %; Oct 2026 calm, 15.6 % and 17.1 %; one year (1-min data, bridged), 24.3 % and 23.6 %. Lab backtests on Binance ETHUSDT at the deployed parameters. Arbitraged blocks, predicted against observed: within 10 %, yet the gap is significant (p < 0.0005). Insurance, not a steady yield.
slides.notes:
Two honest comparisons from a one-year lab backtest on ETH. At the same average fee, clim's LPs lose 27 % less to arbitrage than a fixed-fee pool. At the same cost to traders, 13 % less. The live desk has priced a real storm too: on 7 October 2026 (slide 11), the fee followed volatility up to 26.5 basis points while the fixed pool stayed at 5.11. In money terms: in the lab's main scenario, where an aggregator routes traders between the clim pool and a four times deeper 5 basis point pool, an ETH LP earns about 0.4 % of capital a year more than with a flat 5 basis point fee, about half of it in the five stormiest weeks; across five scenarios, from minus 0.10 % to plus 0.70 %. It is insurance, not a steady yield. These are lab backtests, not audited, and the desk reports every 30 seconds, so the first move of a sudden jump is still arbitraged at the old fee. Fees that rise with volatility are not new: my design research counted at least fifteen, including LiquidMind, built on CRE at Chainlink's Convergence hackathon. What is new here is that the fee comes from a model that makes a prediction anyone can check: how often the pool gets arbitraged. In the February storm and the October calm, the observed share lands within 10 % of the prediction. The gap is still statistically significant, and I say so. And the model is right about how often, not how much: in the backtests, losses run about 1.3 times its estimate.

Sources (not read aloud): lab/out/backtest-summary.json and README Results: -26.9 % and -12.7 % (Oct 2025 to Oct 2026, 1-min data bridged to 12 s blocks); Feb storm -15.3 % and -2.9 %; 92 rolling 4 h windows from -18.4 % to +3.1 %, median -2.1 %, 66 of 92 beat the fixed pool; LP gain +0.39 %/yr in the main scenario (-0.10 % to +0.70 % across 5 scenarios), 53 % of it in the 5 stormiest weeks; lab/out/pstar_decision.json (aggregator scenario, 4x deeper static 5 bp pool). The 7 October live storm: /replay#latest on the live app, computed from the live desk's RiskReported and the pools' Swap events (σ peak 242.1 %/yr in report 1119, V's fee 5.00 to 26.50 bp, S 5.11 bp). The lab replay of 4 February 2026 (not in the spoken part): lab/out/replay-2026-02-04.json (12:00 to 16:00 UTC, σ from 34 % to 296 %/yr, clim fee from 5 to 32.4 bp, fixed pool at 15 bp, replayStaticFeePips 1503 in shared/params.json); the window was picked during design, at P* = 10 %, around the sharpest rise in hourly volatility of the storm (spec section 8). It also ran on Sepolia through a second CRE loop to a replay desk flagged REPLAY, 0x4b843dc3A7ec6202d2337cdeF8C67a0F10f24746 (459 reports from 17:02 to 20:58 UTC on 2026-10-06, loop started at 16:57); its reports come from historical Binance prices served under all four exchange names, so its four sources are not four independent venues. Limits: README Limits and Results (lab backtests on Binance ETHUSDT; not audited; 30 s reporting, so the first move of a jump is arbitraged at the old fee). Prediction: spec section 11 (prior art: LiquidMind, Tempest, Bunni v2, Arrakis Pro, Alphix and Fables, Meteora DLMM, found in pre-hack and design research); lab/out/validation.json (p < 0.0005 with thresholds simulated from the model, because arbitrage comes in clusters); severity 1.29 to 1.33 in lab/out/summary.json.

slides.title: Live since 6 October; why Chainlink CRE, and our feedback
slides.text: Chainlink CRE · our only partner track, by choice. Why CRE, and our feedback. Live since 6 Oct: {{LIVE_SEQ}} CRE reports on Sepolia (RiskDesk seq, read {{LIVE_SEQ_READ}}), and a real storm priced on 7 Oct. Why we built on it. At least 3 of 4 exchanges must report; if they disagree, the fee goes safe. On a DON, workflow ID pinned and owner renounced: no single key. One number for every pool and chain. What we told Chainlink. Smooth: setup, docs, the consensus API. Hard: a multi-node median every 30 s. Ask: show rejected reports in simulation. Today: CRE simulation on one node; our operator key submits the reports.
slides.notes:
All of this runs on Ethereum's Sepolia testnet. Since 6 October at 16:26 UTC, my CRE loop has written about one report every 30 seconds to the live risk desk: {{LIVE_SEQ}} reports when I read it. In 36 hours I built the CRE workflow, the two contracts, the bots that trade on the clim pool and on a fixed-fee twin, the lab that chose the parameters, and the dashboard. And it has already met a real storm: on 7 October around 2 a.m. UTC, ETH moved fast, the desk's volatility climbed to 242 % a year, and the hook raised the fee on pool V to 26.5 basis points, then let it fall back to the floor within the hour. If the desk goes quiet or the exchanges disagree, the LPs stay covered: after three minutes of silence, or when the exchanges disagree, the hook charges at least 30 basis points, and the desk refuses reports from fewer than three exchanges. A false report is bounded, not prevented: volatility can fall at most 20 % per report, and today my operator key is the only sender, until a DON takes over. A forged report I sent was mined and ignored. You can try it yourself: take test tokens from the faucet, swap, and add liquidity. It is a testnet build: my own bots make the market, and the CRE workflow runs in the simulator, on one node; access to deploy it on a Chainlink network was requested but not granted during the hackathon. Chainlink CRE is the only partner track I entered, on purpose: clim is a CRE workflow, not an integration bolted on, and without a fresh CRE report the hook falls back to its safe fee. Insurance needs a weather station everyone trusts. The honest answer first: a volatility measured inside the pool would capture most of the gain in my backtests, so CRE buys trust, not accuracy. Chainlink's own ETH volatility feeds use a 24-hour window with a one-hour heartbeat, so a one-hour storm barely moves them, and Data Streams are pulled by the user, so the swapper could pick which report to bring. CRE runs my own 15-minute estimate and pushes one report every 30 seconds. At least three of the four exchanges must report, and if they disagree, the fee goes safe, so nobody can move the fee with fake trades on the pool. On a DON, the nodes agree on the median of every field and sign one report; once the desk pins our workflow ID, simulation is disabled and I renounce ownership, there is no single key to steal. And one desk can serve every pool and every chain. Today the workflow runs in simulation, on one node, and my operator key submits the reports. What we told Chainlink: setup and docs were smooth, the consensus API worked the first time, and simulate with broadcast gave us a live testnet product without a DON. The hard part: we could not exercise a multi-node median inside each 30-second cycle, because the simulator runs one node; a single node keeps the cadence but loses the decentralization. Our top ask: in simulation, a report the desk rejects looks like a success, so show it as rejected.

Sources (not read aloud): the storm, from the live desk's RiskReported events: fee above the 5 bp floor from 01:58 to 02:51 UTC on 2026-10-07 (100 reports), σ peak 242 %/yr and fee 26.50 bp at 02:11 UTC; live RiskDesk 0xCDbfd6b9C0b97A8eE31706c6CDE5E54B4954334F (state().seq read {{LIVE_SEQ_READ}}); first report 2026-10-06 16:26 UTC, tx https://sepolia.etherscan.io/tx/0x6046552302b7711c4987ee7706d957538dc11ee77ca557b18c92261154e21cb6; latency from observation time (tObs) to block, median 14 s, p90 25 s over 211 reports (cre/README.md); 459 more reports on the replay desk; every transaction, and the workflow's own log lines from a few runs (not the CLI's full output): https://github.com/DVB-ANS/clim/tree/main/docs/evidence. Safety: contracts/src/RiskDesk.sol (reports at least 20 s apart, at most 30 s in the future, quorum 3, volatility at most x2 up and x0.8 down per report, DEGRADED above 25 bp dispersion) and contracts/src/ClimHook.sol (blind after 180 s, safe fee 3000 pips = 30 bp), with their Foundry tests; blind mode shown on 2026-10-06 (the 30.00 bp safe fee quoted 218 s after the last report, docs/sessions/2026-10-06.md); forged report tx https://sepolia.etherscan.io/tx/0x34ee46a6947d2831fdb3e5a09f831008589efd9cf099f61dca86dc4cdadc53d9 (status 1, ReportProcessed false, no RiskReported, desk unchanged). Trust today: in simulation the operator key, which is also the owner, is the only accepted sender, so it decides the volatility within that envelope, and the fee stays between 5 and 150 bp; the owner has no setter for the volatility or the fee; the DON condition is under "Why CRE and our feedback" below. Built: workflow in TypeScript compiled to WASM (cre/risk-desk), contracts in Solidity with Foundry tests (contracts/), bots in Bun and viem (bots/), Python lab (lab/), Next.js dashboard (app/); dashboard https://clim-zeta.vercel.app; verified on Sourcify at the level "match" (partial: metadata hash differs): both desks, both hooks, tETH, tUSD and the arbitrage router. Limits of the live build (README Limits): testnet only, our own bots make the market; a report every 30 s on Ethereum mainnet would cost about 184 ETH of gas a year per gwei (about 175k gas per report, the median of the live Sepolia runs in bots/out/cre-runs.jsonl, times about 1.05 million reports a year, before the production forwarder's signature checks), so production would publish on deviation plus a heartbeat, or on a layer 2; on sub-second chains the formula sits at the floor until an effective block time is calibrated. Why CRE and our feedback: README "Why Chainlink CRE" (in-pool volatility captures 54 % to 103 % of the gain, lab/out/summary.json); Chainlink's ETH realized-volatility Data Feeds have a 24 h shortest window and a 1 h heartbeat, and Data Streams are pull-based, so the swapper picks the report (docs/faq.md, "Why Chainlink CRE, and not Data Feeds or Data Streams?"); quorum and safe fee: at least 3 of the 4 venues with fresh prices or no report (cre/risk-desk/estimator.ts, MIN_SOURCES = 3 in contracts/src/RiskDesk.sol), a report with a venue more than 25 bp from the median is stored but flagged DEGRADED and the hook charges at least its 30 bp safe fee (contracts/src/ClimHook.sol); consensus: ConsensusAggregationByFields with median on each of the seven observation fields (cre/risk-desk/workflow.ts). The DON condition in full (README Roadmap): the owner points RiskDesk at the KeystoneForwarder and pins the expected workflow ID (ReceiverTemplate's identity checks), then calls disableSim() and renounces ownership; until then the owner key can re-point the forwarder. CRE evidence: {{LIVE_SEQ}} simulated reports on the live desk (state().seq read {{LIVE_SEQ_READ}}) and 459 on the replay desk, each from a cre workflow simulate --broadcast run through Chainlink's MockKeystoneForwarder on Sepolia; the workflow uses a 30 s cron trigger, HTTP calls on each node (four exchanges, Deribit DVOL, a USDT/USD rate), median consensus, runtime.report and EVMClient.writeReport, then a read-back of RiskDesk.state(); DON deploy access requested on 2026-10-06 at 22:56 SGT and not granted during the hackathon, so the DON deployment was cut. Our feedback: docs/feedback/cre-devex-report.md (what worked well: installing and setting up CRE, the consensus API working the first time, simulate --broadcast giving a live product without a DON; the hard part, under its ask 3: one node could not show whether several nodes' fetches and their median fit inside each 30 s cron cycle; top ask 1, "A rejected report looks like a success": with --broadcast the write reply says SUCCESS whenever the forwarder transaction is mined, even when the consumer rejected the report; ask 2: the sports-resolution starter's ReceiverTemplate expects 62 bytes of metadata where forwarders pass 64) and the full friction log, docs/feedback/cre-friction-log.md.

slides.title: Roadmap: not a new DEX, a fee engine for existing ones
slides.text: Fables on Robinhood Chain. Not a new DEX. A fee engine for existing ones. 1 Fables markets dynamic fees: its keeper reads the desk. 2 Sepolia first, then every EVM chain CRE supports. 3 Next: volume next to volatility, as market makers price it. Roadmap, our proposal to Fables: nothing runs on Robinhood Chain yet. Sofiane Ben Taleb, solo builder · DeVinci Blockchain · github.com/DVB-ANS/clim. QR code: Try it, clim-zeta.vercel.app.
slides.notes:
clim is not a new DEX. It is a risk desk, the CRE workflow and its on-chain contract, plus a hook pattern that existing protocols plug in: their keeper or their hook reads the desk and applies the fee rule with their own parameters. Fables comes first: it already presents its fees as dynamic, and a keeper moves them between a floor and a cap. We start in shadow mode, clim's fee next to the keeper's, tuned for Robinhood Chain's fast blocks; then their keeper reads the desk and posts the fee, with no contract change on their side. This is my proposal to Fables, not an agreement: nothing runs on Robinhood Chain yet. A pool that is already live cannot just flip to clim: a static-fee pool means a new pool, while a DEX whose keeper posts the fee, like Fables, can use the desk without migrating. Sepolia is where I prove it; every EVM chain CRE supports comes next. The next input is the pool's own volume, next to volatility, priced the way market makers price it: when volume is thin, a lower fee brings traders back; when one-way, informed flow dominates, the fee rises. It would enter through k, the multiplier the desk already sends in every report, so the hook would not change; in this build k is clamped between 1 and 2, so it can only raise the fee. I am Sofiane Ben Taleb, from DeVinci Blockchain in Paris, and I built clim solo at TOKEN2049 Origins. Everything is public, including a friction log and a DevEx report for the Chainlink team. The QR code opens the app, and the full demo video is the submission's Project link. Thank you.

Sources (not read aloud): README Roadmap and Limits (fast chains: the formula sits at the floor until an effective block time is calibrated); spec section 5 (Fables: flat fee plus keeper pokeFee overrides between a floor and a cap, read from public on-chain data on 2026-09-30); Robinhood Chain's blocks are much shorter than Sepolia's 12 s, so the fee is tuned for them in shadow mode first; spec section 5.6 (a keeper is off-chain, so it can read a RiskDesk on any chain where CRE writes); CRE lists Robinhood Chain as a testnet only (docs, 2026-09-18). A pool that is already live, the Chainlink mentor's second question on 6 October: docs/faq.md ("Can a pool that is already live switch to clim?": a v3 pool's fee is immutable; a static-fee v4 pool cannot become dynamic or gain a hook; a dynamic-fee v4 pool follows the desk only if its hook can read an external source or exposes a keeper path to updateDynamicLPFee, otherwise a new hook means a new pool; a keeper-set DEX like Fables reads RiskDesk.state() with no contract change; clim's own parameters are immutable, so a new P* means a new hook and a new pool), checked against v4-core and OpenZeppelin uniswap-hooks v1.2.1. Volume: README Roadmap item 4 and docs/faq.md ("Why not set the fee from volume too?", a judge's suggestion at the booth on 7 October 2026): not in this build (the workflow sends k = 1); the workflow would read the clim pool's recent Swap events with CRE's EVM client, split arbitrage from uninformed flow and raise k with the arbitrage share; RiskDesk clamps k to [1, 2] (K_MIN_E4 10000, K_MAX_E4 20000), so it can only raise the storm premium, and a fee cut needs a desk that accepts k below 1, so a new hook and new pools (the hook's desk address is immutable); grounded in market-making theory: a spread pays the market maker for trading with better-informed traders (Glosten and Milgrom 1985), and a market maker's quotes depend on volatility and on how order arrivals respond to the spread (Avellaneda and Stoikov 2008); not a sure win, since a higher DEX fee can raise volume by paying LPs to supply depth (Hasbrouck, Rivera and Saleh 2022, "The Need for Fees at a DEX: How Increases in Fees Can Increase DEX Trading Volume"); the lab would backtest it at the same average fee and at the same cost to traders, with the predicted share of arbitraged blocks 1/(k × η + 0.824). Team: Sofiane Ben Taleb, solo (docs/submission/team.json); https://github.com/DVB-ANS/clim; https://clim-zeta.vercel.app; docs/feedback/cre-devex-report.md and docs/feedback/cre-friction-log.md. The full demo video is on Google Drive and is the Project link of the Builderbase submission (videoUrl in docs/submission/links.json).
